title: The Watch in the Glove
markdown:
Leo really disliked surprises. Sudden rustles of leaves made him jump, pop quizzes felt like traps, and surprise parties? He thought they were elaborate schemes designed to make him look silly. His days were best when they followed a calm, predictable path, like a perfectly wound clock. Elara, his friend, was different. She was an apprentice watchmaker, her world already a dance of tiny gears and measured seconds. She found comfort in things that were clear and orderly.

Today, their feet were on the old platform of Oakhaven Station. Cobwebs, like forgotten lace, clung to the rusty signs. The air smelled heavy and damp, like wet earth with a ghost of coal smoke. A poster, its colours faded by many years, advertised train times from 1928. Next to it, a modern digital display, usually showing train arrivals, blinked with today’s date. It felt like two different worlds had just brushed past each other on this quiet stretch of track.

“That’s strange,” Elara whispered. Her fingers traced a thin crack in the old poster. “This is for the ‘Oakhaven Flyer’ to Willow Creek. And this screen,” she pointed to the digital advertisement, “has a special alert about a lost package. Both mention Oakhaven Station, but one is from almost a hundred years ago.”

Leo looked closer at the poster. Its old-fashioned letters boasted of being on time and comfortable. “‘Special delivery,’ it says here. For Mr. Silas Croft. ‘Handle with great care.’” He scrunched up his nose. “What do you think it was?”

Elara, always so careful, saw a faint, almost invisible smudge of ink under the date on the poster. “It looks like another date, written quickly. August 14th, 1928.” Then she tapped the digital screen. “And this alert… it’s also for a delivery to Silas Croft, supposed to arrive today. The package is… a pocket watch.”

Leo’s stomach did a little flip-flop, the kind he didn’t like. A surprise delivery, a hundred years apart? This was exactly the kind of unpredictable mess he found so annoying. But Elara’s focused curiosity was like a gentle stream, pulling him along. “So,” Leo said, a spark of interest lighting up his eyes, “they both wanted to deliver this watch to Silas Croft. One is already lost, and the other needs to be found. That sounds like a pretty interesting puzzle.”

Elara nodded, her brow furrowed in thought. She took out a small, shiny magnifying glass from her pocket. “The poster has some odd words. ‘A stitch in time, a hasty rhyme, will see the treasure in its prime.’” She paused, thinking. “And in smaller letters below: ‘If the conductor forgets his glove, the trunk holds more than just his love.’”

Leo let out a small, dry chuckle. “What on earth could that mean? What conductor would forget his glove? And how does a trunk connect to a pocket watch?”

“It’s a riddle,” Elara said, though even she sounded unsure. “Or maybe it’s a joke that people don’t get anymore.” Elara often misplaced things herself. “It reminds me of when I can’t find my favorite polishing cloth. It just disappears! I always say, ‘Where has my little cloth flown?’ It’s a silly thought, but it makes me feel a little better.”

Their eyes swept across the platform. Among the old benches and fallen autumn leaves, a large, dark, leather-bound trunk sat near the far end. It looked as old and worn as the station itself. Its brass clasps shone dimly, and its sturdy handle was marked from many journeys.

“That trunk,” Leo said, pointing. “It looks like it’s been here since the station was built. Maybe Silas Croft left it here.”

“The riddle mentioned a conductor,” Elara mused, her eyes fixed on the poster. “And a forgotten glove. In 1928, conductors would have worn gloves, and they were in charge of passengers’ luggage.” She looked at the poster again. “The clue about the glove… it’s meant to show *where* the watch is hidden. But it only makes sense if you understand the joke.”

Suddenly, Leo’s mind, which usually resisted the unexpected, started working in a new way. “Wait a minute,” he said, a slow smile spreading across his face. “I think I get it. That joke wasn't about *forgetting* his glove. It was about *finding* it in a funny way. Imagine this: a conductor, rushing around, probably carrying a lot of things. He has his watch, his ticket, and his gloves. He might put his watch down, maybe to adjust his hat. Then, he reaches for his gloves, but he’s holding so much, he accidentally tucks his watch deep inside one of his gloves. Then, he puts that glove, watch and all, into a trunk. It would have been a funny, slightly silly mistake. Everyone would have seen it happening.”

As Leo spoke, the air around them seemed to shimmer. For just a moment, the platform looked like an old photograph, tinted brown. A younger man, wearing the smart uniform of a train conductor, hurried past. He looked a little frustrated. In one hand, he held a pair of dark gloves. He glanced back quickly, then, with a swift movement, opened the large trunk. He fumbled inside for a second, then hurried away, leaving the trunk a little open. The vision vanished as quickly as it had appeared, leaving them back in the present.

Elara gasped, her eyes wide. “You mean… the joke *itself* is the place? The conductor put his watch *inside* his glove, and then put the glove *into* the trunk?”

“Exactly!” Leo exclaimed, a wave of unexpected warmth and satisfaction washing over him. It wasn't the surprise that felt good, but the feeling of understanding. He walked over to the trunk. Its heavy lid creaked as he lifted it. Inside, resting among what looked like old, moth-eaten blankets, were a pair of worn leather gloves. He carefully reached into one of them, his fingers touching something small and cool. He pulled it out.

It was a pocket watch, beautifully carved, its silver case catching the dim light with a soft gleam. It still ticked, a steady, reassuring beat against his palm.

“We found it,” Elara whispered, her voice full of quiet wonder.

Leo looked at the watch, then at Elara. “You know,” he said, his voice softer now, “history isn’t just about big events or famous speeches. It’s made up of small moments. Like a conductor who made a silly mistake, and a joke that helped someone find something important.” He held out the watch. “And maybe,” he added, a small smile on his lips, “it’s also about friends who don’t mind going on a little unexpected adventure together.”

Elara gently took the watch, her fingers fitting perfectly around its smooth, cool surface. “Where has my little cloth flown?” she murmured, a private joke now shared between them. The ticking of the watch seemed to echo the quiet, steady rhythm of everyday courage that, through all the years, had kept time moving forward. They left the platform, and the old station slowly returned to its silent, dusty sleep. The faint smell of damp earth and coal smoke was a gentle reminder of the many untold stories hidden within its old walls.
characters: boy who hates surprises, a watchmaker's apprentice
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
